title: {{NAME}} and the Princess of the Cretaceous Court
moral: The most impressive thing you can do with power is use it to make space for someone else.

pages.content:
The Cretaceous Court was neither in the past nor entirely in the present: it existed in that particular sliver of time that only opens on midsummer nights when the fog comes in low and the old standing stones on the hill catch the light at exactly the right angle. {{NAME}} had read about it in a library book that the librarian herself had not catalogued, shelved in the wrong section entirely, which was how books of this kind were generally kept safe.

He arrived through the fog and found himself in a courtyard of enormous ferns surrounding a stone hall roofed with living vines. The court was in session. Dinosaurs attended in remarkable numbers: a pair of velociraptor lords standing to one side with the patient dignity of those accustomed to formal proceedings, three small small dinosaur scribes taking notes on broad leaves with sharp sticks, and at the centre of the courtyard, managing all of it with effortless authority, a princess.

Princess Corvina was perhaps twelve years old, wore a crown of woven fern and carved amber, and was in the middle of a precise, patient disagreement with an velociraptor lord three times her height. She was clearly winning.

pages.content:
Corvina noticed {{NAME}} the moment his boot scraped on the stone. She had that quality of attention that noticed everything and forgot nothing, and she paused her argument just long enough to look him over completely before addressing the velociraptor again and winning the disagreement within two further sentences.

Then she walked over to {{NAME}} with the direct, no-ceremony approach of someone who has never found ceremony useful.

'You're from outside,' she said. 'The compass gives it away. Inside the court the compass points to the oldest creature in the room, which is currently Lord Fen.' She nodded at the taller velociraptor, who inclined his massive head with austere acknowledgment. 'Can you read old maps?'

{{NAME}}'s face broke into pure, startled delight. He had been reading old maps since he was four. He had seventeen of them on his bedroom wall. He reached for the compass, the needle swinging steadily toward Lord Fen, and looked up at Corvina with eyes that said yes before his mouth did.

Corvina's composed expression shifted into something that was not quite a smile but was the thing that happens just before a smile, something better, in some ways, than the smile itself.

pages.content:
The map in question was a problem of considerable urgency. One of the three young small dinosaur scribes had gone missing in the court's extensive underground archive while chasing a misfiled scroll. The archive was a labyrinth of root-tunnels and carved passages that had been expanded without plan over several hundred years, and its original map, the only one that showed the whole system, was in a script Corvina could not read.

But {{NAME}} could. It was an old navigational shorthand, used by coastal cartographers, and he had learned it from the wrong-section library book's appendix three weeks ago for no particular reason. The universe, he had noticed, frequently arranged this kind of thing.

He and Corvina entered the archive together, {{NAME}} with the map unfolded between his hands, Corvina with a torch of compressed fern-light, Lord Fen's massive bulk waiting at the entrance because he would not fit.

The tunnels were extraordinary: smooth-walled and warm, the roots of the courtyard ferns forming a vaulted ceiling above them, the floor packed earth with fossilised impressions of footsteps that had been pressed there an unimaginable time ago.

pages.content:
They found the young small dinosaur scribe, whose name was Pip, three levels down in a circular chamber that the archive's builder had clearly been particularly proud of, given its ornate carved ceiling. Pip had not been distressed at all. She had found the misfiled scroll, read it from beginning to end, and then found fourteen other interesting scrolls and was methodically working through them all.

She looked up when the torch-light found her with the expression of someone interrupted in the middle of something very good.

Corvina stood in the chamber doorway and looked at Pip for a long moment. Then she looked at {{NAME}}. Then she looked at the fourteen scrolls spread around Pip in a careful organised circle.

'She alphabetised them,' {{NAME}} observed.

'She did,' Corvina agreed.

They carried the scrolls back up together, all three of them, {{NAME}} and Corvina each with an armful, Pip carrying two and leading the way with absolute confidence. At the archive entrance Lord Fen lowered his enormous head so that Pip could climb up and be deposited at her scribe station by the most dignified possible route.

pages.content:
The court reassembled in the evening with the scrolls installed in their correct places, Pip at her station, and the whole enterprise of the Cretaceous Court resumed exactly where it had paused, which was the business of making sure ancient and modern things continued to understand each other.

Corvina gave {{NAME}} a copy of the archive map, hand-copied by Pip onto a fresh leaf with the original shorthand preserved. It was the best gift he had ever been given and he held it as carefully as if it were made of light.

The velociraptor lords settled into their evening rest positions: seated, enormous, still as hills. The small dinosaur scribes rolled their leaf-notes and tucked them into their carrying pouches. The ferns above the courtyard rustled in a rising midsummer wind.

{{NAME}} sat on a warm stone bench with the map across his knees, and the fog at the court's entrance began to thicken, the way it did when time was gently suggesting a door was opening.

Corvina sat beside him. Neither spoke. The compass pointed to Lord Fen, steady and certain.

Goodnight, cartographer. Sleep warm, and wonder what the fourteenth scroll contained.
